description: Buscamos innovar e integrar las tradiciones de nuestra comunidad educativa
summary:
We developed a web app that turns 21 agricultural knowledge practices from the IE El Placer community (Ipiales Indigenous Reserve, Nariño) into decision rules of the form “if this happens, then do this.” The app compares them with 25 years of NASA POWER data and shows each piece of knowledge on a two-sided card: what the elders say and what NASA sees, with a status that indicates how much support it has.

It addresses the Field Shift challenge by helping each family decide when to plant and what to rotate in a changing climate (+0.7 °C since the 1980s, and annual rainfall ranging from 737 to 1,613 mm). It matters because it protects the memory of an Indigenous people, and it honestly acknowledges what satellites cannot measure, such as frosts and the moon. The app supports the word of the elders and does not replace it.
details:
What exactly does it do? The user marks their plot on a map and answers three questions: whether they have irrigation, what they planted before, and whether they can count on a minga (community work party). With that, they receive the wheel of the year, alerts for blight, frost and erosion, and three compared rotations. They can also keep a planting log.

How does it work? The knowledge is stored in a rules file (reglas.json) and the data in el-placer.json. A JavaScript engine of about 80 lines cross-checks both, with tests for the four cases. Each piece of advice comes with its source, the data that supports it, the size of that data, and one of five statuses: Confirmed, Risk, Difference to review, Not measurable by satellite, or To validate with elders.

What are the benefits? Families receive advice that is explainable and checked against data. The museum and the school gain an intercultural teaching tool. Judges and the community can see when the data confirms a piece of knowledge and when it falls short.

What do we hope to achieve? That each family decides together with their elders, using data that explains the why. We also want to validate the pending rules, such as the lunar ones, with the community, and to add frosts using nighttime surface temperature.

What tools did we use? Python to download the data, JavaScript for the rules engine and the screens, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap for the map, SunCalc to calculate the moon phase in the browser, and Netlify for publishing.

A note on terms: I kept “minga” and explained it in parentheses, since it is a specific Andean practice with no exact English equivalent. I also translated “gota” as “blight” (late blight of potato), which is the usual English term for that disease.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) – daily and climatology data, AG community
NASA Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) – 1 arc-second elevation
